Narrator: Vira Toland (born 1912, recorded at Ostrey Hollow in 1979). Gist: in 1919 the Association's manager Selby Vose sent a letter accusing nine families of watering their milk, which split the Keddie and Brant families; the tests later rose with no explanation, a hearing at Ashlin removed tester Ansel Keddie and paid the patrons $3,500, and Vira believes he was stealing the cream.
The report doesn't mention 1908: it covers 1966 and recommends a levy of six mills on the dollar for 1967, one mill less than the 1966 levy.

Narrator: Effie Loomis, the Association's secretary from 1901 to 1940, writing numbered notes in 1941. Gist: from the minutes, she records Article VII's rule that the station's own butterfat test governs, the patrons' 1925 petition, and the Ashlin board under Alonzo Frick, which found "no cause established" yet awarded $3,800. She adds that nobody in the office ever watched the station work, and that the measures condemned in June 1923 were never mentioned at the hearing.
The play at the Ellerby Playhouse is *The Sparrow Hotel*.

Narrator: Ansel Keddie, the Ostrey Hollow tester, in his nine-sentence statement to the Ashlin board (17 March 1925) and an unsent letter from that spring. Gist: he denies taking any cream and describes his exact testing routine and book. The station averaged 3.61 from 1898 on, but 3.80 whenever borrowed glass was used (1896 and nine weeks in 1911) and again in 1924. He also covers the 1902 complaints, the 1908 wet-hay report and the 1919 circular, his rift with Emmet Brant, and being put out on 30 April.
The day-book records the Purcell & Weare order of 14 March 1932 as $59.65 on sixty days' credit, though its listed items actually add up to $56.15.

Narrator: Ivy Keddie, Ansel's granddaughter, giving a 1959 talk to the Ordell County Historical Society. Gist: the station's 1897 pipettes, condemned in 1923 and found in a crate in the loft, delivered 16.72 c.c. against 17.6, so every test read 95% of the truth. That understated the patrons' butterfat by 76,000 lb (about $19,000) between 1898 and 1922, which the ledgers booked as "station gain," against a $3,800 award. The 1911 borrowed-measure weeks, Bulletin 214's wet-hay result and the Alder Corners figures all back this up, and Bulletin 471 (1958) clears Keddie.
Tamsin Ochoa's service number is 4471-K.

Narrator: Wilbur Teague, the Association's bookkeeper from 1905 to 1945, in a 1948 memoir chapter. Gist: he explains the "station gain" line of about 5¼%, which Vose signed every year and told him to let alone in 1916, and gives the station figures his way: 44 million lb of milk, a 3.16 average test, and a six-week borrowed measure in 1911. He still argues that cream is portable and one unwatched man could take it, and records the $3,800 award "without admission."
Delia Fought was fined $5.00 for taking dress goods worth $2.40, the court citing the small value and her clean record.

Narrator: Merle Strawn, the retired state dairy inspector, copying extracts from his 28 circuit books (1907–1936) with a covering note. Gist: on every visit to Ostrey Hollow he found true scales and no added water, and told the manager so after the 1919 circular. He watched a test in June 1911 and noted nothing. After receiving a burette in 1921, he condemned the whole crate of station pipettes on 12 June 1923 because they would not deliver their mark. The new glass checked true that October, and tests were improved in 1924 (3.80) and 1925. He records only facts, never opinions.
Lemma 2.1 is named "Interleaving."

Narrator: Halbert Nym, curator, in his 1972 accession notes for the Ordell County dairy collection. Gist: he catalogues sixteen items, including Article VII, the 1897 Ammon & Sons invoice ($77.93), the station test book and the Brant weigh book (1910: 200,000 lb paid on a test of 3.42), the pipette crate, the ledgers, the $3,800 award, Strawn's 1923 condemnation, the 1908 committee report, Bulletins 214 and 471, and Ivy's measurement sheet. His notes contain some slips, notably swapped keeper names on Items 3 and 4 and placing the crate's discovery at the Ashlin office.
Ansgar Krell stayed 4 weeks, from 3 May until his discharge on 31 May 1884.

Narrator: Selby Vose, the Association's manager since 1913, in his 1926 annual address to members. Gist: he calls the $3,800 award (after "no cause established") a generous settlement of an unproved claim, blames water in the cans that stopped "when the looking began," and cites a 1924 rise to 3.90. He dismisses the inspector's condemnation of the apparatus, which he dates to 12 July 1923, as housekeeping, defends his 1919 circular, and points to his father's Jersey herd testing 4.56 in 1910. Several of his dates and figures conflict with the other accounts.
A sailings query span longer than 14 days returns error code `SKF-2201` (HTTP 400).

Acknowledged: **Roy Brant**, Emmet Brant's son (1955, with a 1958 postscript), describes his father's Hessel Bottom weigh book. It shows the farm's scale and the station's always agreed, while the Hollow's tests ran a steady 0.17 under Larrow Green's in every season, rose only during the nine borrowed-measure weeks of 1911, and led to the family rift and the book's loan to his cousin's daughter Ivy.
Dr. Pemberton charged $8.00 for Mrs. Content Averill's confinement and mileage on January 3, 1906, and it was paid in full in cash on January 20.

Acknowledged: **Rosalie Cudd**, the Alder Corners cheesemaker and Jerome Cudd's daughter, writes to Ivy Keddie in 1958 that four Hessel Bottom men hauled to her father's factory each summer flush from 1915 to 1930. Their milk, tested on his own new glass, averaged about 3.80 every season (between 3.78 and 3.82) and was never watered, with no one ever comparing those figures against the station's.
After insurance, the man's crown will cost him $1,480, which he says includes the temporary plastic crown.

Acknowledged: **Professor Leland Vaught**, in his October 1958 introduction and method for Bulletin No. 471, argues that a short pipette, which the plant had no way to check, produced a steady, proportional low test at Ostrey Hollow, and treats the nine borrowed-measure weeks of 1911 as a natural experiment. His middle sections contradict his own conclusion. He gives five dozen pipettes, a 16.27 c.c. mean, glass in use from 1 May 1898, and a 0.295 shortfall worth 118,000 lb. His conclusion keeps one part in twenty and 76,000 lb from 1 May 1897.
The third paragraph names vermilion, the color of the apron Bettine Rausch wears to serve dinner.

Acknowledged: **Dell Rundle**, the Larrow Green schoolteacher, in the 1939 jubilee pamphlet (reprinted 1959), tells the valley's version of the Association's fifty years. It dates Article VII to 1891, calls Selby Vose Gideon's nephew, and records the belief that cream was stolen, along with 12 July 1923, 44M lb and a $19,600 petition figure. A note added in press, after Rundle saw the ledger's yearly 5¼% "station gain," takes back the theft story because stolen cream would have reached the Green light, not heavy. A 1959 footnote says eleven pipettes survive and that Ivy is Hazel Brant's second cousin.
Message No. 219 was 6 words, charged at the $0.25 minimum plus a $0.60 connecting toll, for $0.85 in all.

Acknowledged: **Alonzo Frick**, the board's chairman, looks back in 1946 on the 1925 Ostrey Hollow arbitration. It sat once at Ashlin and twice at the station, heard three unproved theories (Vose on water, Teague implying theft, the 1908 report on hay), and made its 4 May award of $3,800 without a finding, after the Association had already let Keddie go on 30 April. His account and exhibit list conflict with the other accounts: a 3.16 average, a patrons' claim of 67,000 lb, and a private corridor remark that Keddie blamed the patrons. The list shows four books, including Strawn's 1923 notebook and Brant's weigh book, but no glassware.
The locksmith's dog is Buckley, a bad-tempered gray terrier.

Acknowledged: **Hobart Sill**, the retiring Larrow Green buttermaker (1893–1934, age 64), says the Hollow's cream always came in heavier than the station's sheets showed, but he dismisses that as the nature of cream. He still blames water because the Hollow's tests rose "one summer in the twenties." He claims his own glass opened the station in May 1896, and he gives Larrow Green's average as 3.78 against the Hollow's "real" 3.85, fat at 27¢, and about 900,000 lb of intake in the first season.
Definition 1.3 defines the Trebbin norm, written ‖(x_k)‖_T.

Acknowledged: **Nyle Grigg**, chairman of the 1908 committee, reissues its report in 1919 with a covering letter defending the wet-hay finding, which cleared everyone of dishonesty. The letter misstates the record twice. It claims sampling every month of 1908, though the report says January–March only, and it says Bulletin 214 found a two-tenths depression in winter, where the bulletin says at most 0.05. He also dates payment by test to 1893 and puts six farms on Hessel Bottom.
API level 31 removes the level-27 accessor `chart.rawCells()`, and code should use `chart.at(row, col)` or `chart.slice(sel)` instead.

Acknowledged: **Dr. Roland Kepp**, an Ashlin veterinary surgeon, argues in his 1926 Farm Club paper that Hessel Bottom's sour wet ground explains the station's low tests, and he waves off the station as a possible cause. He gives the gap as 0.21 and says Bulletin 214 found two tenths in winter, when it says at most 0.05 and nothing on summer pasture. He calls the 1911 borrowed-measure interval six weeks of flush-season figures, and prices fat at 27¢.
Phyl warns Armando not to use dryer number eleven, which takes your money, turns for about forty seconds and then stops.

Read r17: Hazel Brant, Roy's daughter and the last keeper of the weigh book, recorded in 1981. She says she remembers quantities but not years, and retells the family story: the 1910 leaf of 200,000 lb even at 3.42, a flat 0.19 gap, the crate found in the loft, and the claim that she and Ivy are second cousins.
The color named in the third paragraph is magenta: the woman called Tuesday wears a magenta scarf in all weathers.

Read r18: Duncan Keddie, Ansel's son and a retired Ashlin schoolteacher, writing family notes in 1968 with a 1970 addition. He sets out the family connections: Orra was Emmet's sister, Hazel and Ivy are second cousins, Selby was Gideon's son, and there was no Vose kinship. He recalls his father suspecting "the glass" in 1911, and he traces where each book and the crate ended up.

The jury found that Obadiah Chalmers drowned in the Colquitt Bros. mill pond on the night of 12 January 1927 after an accidental fall from the flume edge while at work, with no evidence that anyone else was involved, and it recommended fitting a rail or footing plank there.

Read r19: *The Ashlin Chronicle*'s front-page feature of 3 October 1958, rushed out from a press release and two phone calls. It celebrates Bulletin 471 for clearing Ansel Keddie through the crate Ivy found in the loft, and it garbles many details: it calls Ivy his great-niece and Rosalie a niece, and it gives eleven pipettes, a 16.27 mean, $19,600 owed and $77.39 for the outfit.
The ice-out pot in the spring of 1996 was $6,840, half of it for the fire department and half for the closest guess.

Read r20: Junia Ammon, the firm's historian, in chapter nine of the 1949 Ammon & Sons history. She reproduces the 14 April 1897 invoice and the 2 July 1923 letter, blames a reground mold that made the lot consistently short, and regrets how thin the letter was. Her own text contradicts itself: the invoice totals $77.93 but her prose says $77.39, and she writes that the firm "sold nothing into Ordell County before 1900" despite that 1897 sale.
The sharpness example in Proposition 4.1 uses a 7-cycle, with a pendant path of length two attached to each vertex.

Read r21: Cleve Oram, the cream hauler's son (born 1900), recorded at Larrow Green in 1977. He describes the road, the station and the crate in the loft over the intake room, and the 1925 hearing: one sitting at Ashlin, two in the weigh room. He repeats his father's belief that cream went missing. He also garbles figures and kin: five dozen pipettes, a $3,500 award, 67,000 lb, Ivy as Hazel's first cousin once removed, and a Keddie–Vose kinship.
A BSWP frame starts with the delimiter byte `0xB5` and ends with `0x5B`.

Read r22: county agent Orin Falke's 1959 numbered report to the Ordell County board. It lays out the case: 1896 opening, a 0.19 gap in every month, the nine weeks of 1911, three failed theories, the 12 June 1923 condemnation, and nine pipettes measured 9 March 1958, though it gives 3.85 from 1924. In an added note, after reading Bulletin 214's summary (at most 0.05 in winter, nothing in summer), Falke withdraws his concession to the hay theory and corrects Ivy from great-niece to granddaughter.
Russ's wife is named Dorrit, after her mother's mother.

Read r23: Bertram Kyle, a retired clerk who for 25 years sat at the outer desk outside the manager's door, writing for the Historical Society in 1953. His point is that the "station gain, five and a quarter per cent, as usual" line sat in plain sight every year with a name on it, and nobody set the receiving book beside Strawn's notebook among the four books given to the board. He also misdates several things: the Larrow Green office, own glass from 1 May 1898, about 1.1M lb in the first season, Selby as manager from 1911, Strawn's visit in 1922, and the award in 1924.
The third paragraph names teal, the colour of the endpapers of the collected edition that carry Halvane's diagram.

Read r24: Orra Keddie's farm diary for 1897–1930, published in 1964 with a loose leaf from 1934. It shows the household side of the case: own glass on 1 May 1897, the four-man committee in January 1908, the broken measure on 8 May 1911, Ansel carrying the 1919 circular himself to eleven families, and Emmet's estrangement over it. It then covers the 1925 sittings and dismissal, Ansel's later life as a carpenter and his death in February 1934, and his saying that "a man cannot be cleared of a thing nobody will name."
The toll collected at Wren's Bend bridge for 5–11 June 1899 was $13.88; the day totals add up to that, and the $6.00 in annual passes was kept separate.
